claims.claim: U.S. copyright protects original works of authorship fixed in a tangible medium of expression, and protects expression rather than ideas, procedures, methods, systems, or facts.
Copyright protection arises automatically the moment an original work is created and fixed in a tangible medium; registration and a copyright notice are not required for protection to exist.
A copyright owner holds exclusive rights to reproduce the work, prepare derivative works, distribute copies, and publicly display or perform it.
Registration is optional but is a prerequisite to suing for infringement of a U.S. work and can make statutory damages and attorney's fees available; it also creates a public record.

For works created by an individual on or after January 1, 1978, copyright lasts for the life of the author plus 70 years; for works made for hire and anonymous/pseudonymous works, 95 years from publication or 120 years from creation, whichever expires first.

Fair use is a fact-specific doctrine evaluated case by case on four statutory factors: purpose and character of the use (including commercial vs nonprofit educational and transformative use), nature of the work, amount and substantiality used, and effect on the potential market; there is no fixed formula or safe percentage.

The public domain consists of works not protected by copyright (term expired or never eligible); works prepared by U.S. federal government employees as part of official duties are not subject to copyright.

Royalty-free licenses charge a single fee for broad reuse and are typically non-exclusive; rights-managed licenses grant a specific defined use (duration, territory, placement) and can include exclusivity; 'royalty-free' does not mean free of cost.

Model releases (for recognizable people) and property releases (for recognizable private property) are separate permissions addressing privacy and publicity rights and are generally required for commercial use in addition to the image's copyright license.

Under the work-made-for-hire doctrine, the employer or commissioning party is the author/owner for works prepared by an employee within the scope of employment, or for certain specially ordered/commissioned works in enumerated categories with a signed written agreement; otherwise a freelancer generally retains the copyright.
Copyright and trademark protect different things: copyright protects creative expression, while a trademark protects words, symbols, or designs that identify the source of goods or services.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether using an entire copyrighted work can ever be fair use
positions: Larger amounts generally disfavor fair use
Courts have found use of an entire work fair in certain circumstances, and even a small but crucial portion can defeat fair use
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented both: amount is one factor weighed with the others, not a bright line. Sourced to the Copyright Office fair-use overview.

sourceRecords.title: What Is Copyright?
sourceRecords.notes: Supports originality + fixation requirement, expression-not-ideas, automatic protection, and the list of exclusive rights (reproduce, derivative works, distribute, display/perform). U.S. Government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. Copyright Office Fair Use Index / More Information on Fair Use
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the four fair-use factors and the case-by-case, fact-specific nature of the analysis, including that entire-work use can sometimes be fair and small crucial use may not be.

sourceRecords.title: Copyright in General (FAQ)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports automatic protection, registration optional but required before suing / enabling statutory damages, and the copyright vs. trademark vs. patent distinctions (trademark = source identifier).

sourceRecords.title: Duration of Copyright (FAQ)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports duration: life + 70 for post-1978 individual works; 95 years from publication or 120 from creation for works made for hire and anonymous/pseudonymous works.

sourceRecords.title: Circular 1: Copyright Basics
sourceRecords.notes: Supports categories of protected works, automatic securing ('the moment it is created and fixed in a tangible medium'), optional notice format (© year owner), registration benefits, and duration. Read as PDF.

sourceRecords.title: Circular 9: Works Made for Hire
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the two-part work-made-for-hire definition (employee within scope of employment; or specially ordered/commissioned works in enumerated categories with a written agreement) and that the employer/commissioning party is the author/owner. Read as PDF.
